blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Much of the manipulation in online influencer content is not false but disproportionate: an accurate fact is framed as historic, urgent, or catastrophic. Fact-checking and clickbait detection are not designed to capture such framing, and little is known about where it originates: with the creator, the topic, the platform, or the audience that replies. We operationalize rhetorical distortion through five literature-grounded dimensions (Significance Inflation, Anxiety Manufacturing, Novelty Claims, Loaded Language, and Temporal Distortion) and measure it with a three-tier pipeline in which bilingual lexical rules propose candidates, negative filters cancel known false-positive contexts, and an LLM verifies or relabels the candidates. Applying the pipeline to 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on six platforms (RSS/newsletters, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit, Weibo, and X/Twitter), we find that platform is far more strongly associated with account-level distortion than content category (Kruskal-Wallis $\varepsilon^2=0.33$; two-way ANOVA $η_p^2=0.49$ for platform vs. $0.09$ for category). X/Twitter scores highest (DI 7.74 vs. 0.78 for RSS). Classifying tweets and their replies separately shows where this comes from: the reply layer readers see under a post (its top-5 replies) carries 3.5x the distortion of the tweet it answers (7.65 vs. 2.17, $p<10^{-6}$, 36 of 43 accounts), driven by Loaded Language. At equal text length the gap shrinks to 1.5x but remains significant, and creator tweets alone are statistically indistinguishable from YouTube and Bluesky. Two independent human annotators confirm the reply gap, and the platform ordering and the reply gap replicate with GPT-4o as a second classifier. On threaded platforms, measured distortion thus lives largely in the audience layer, which motivates measurement that separates creator and reply text.

blocks.en:
Social media influencers have become primary information intermediaries, and their
content is governed by engagement metrics rather than editorial standards. Consider a
commentator who accurately reports that “markets fell 0.3%” but frames it as
“CATASTROPHIC COLLAPSE—act NOW.” No fact is false, so the post is invisible to
fact-checking pipelines ( Vosoughi et al., 2018 ) . It is not clickbait either, because
nothing is withheld ( Potthast et al., 2016 ; Chen et al., 2015 ) . Yet the framing
overstates the evidential weight of the event and tells the audience how alarmed to be.
This kind of disproportionate framing shapes what audiences believe matters, and
it is produced at scale on every major platform.

blocks.en:
To address these questions, we first define rhetorical distortion through five
dimensions grounded in rhetoric, framing, and fear-appeal theory, and aggregate them
into an account-level Distortion Index (DI) and a separate Consistency Score (CS). We
then build a three-tier detection pipeline (Figure 1 ). Bilingual lexical
rules act as a transparent recall gate that proposes candidate dimensions, negative
filters cancel matches in known false-positive contexts, and an LLM either classifies a
candidate from scratch or verifies the rule labels, depending on the rules’ confidence.
Posts with no rule hit are never sent to the LLM. We apply the pipeline to 13,060 posts
from 330 accounts on six platforms and, on X/Twitter, classify each tweet and its top-5
replies both jointly and separately. We validate the labels with two independent human
annotators, replicate the main results with a second LLM, and analyze the data with
rank-based tests, a two-way ANOVA, post-level logistic regressions that control for text
length, paired tests, and account fixed-effects models.

blocks.en: 2. Background and Related Work
blocks.zh: 2. 背景和有关工作

blocks.en:
Misinformation research asks whether a claim is true and how false claims spread ( Vosoughi et al., 2018 ) . Clickbait detection targets headlines that withhold
information to provoke clicks ( Potthast et al., 2016 ; Chen et al., 2015 ) .
Fine-grained propaganda detection labels techniques such as Loaded Language and
Exaggeration in news articles ( Da San Martino et al., 2019 ; Da San Martino et al., 2020 ) ,
and shared tasks have since extended this to multilingual framing and persuasion ( Piskorski et al., 2023 ) . Earlier lexical work showed that emotional and certainty
markers distinguish unreliable from reliable news ( Rashkin et al., 2017 ) . We borrow
these techniques but apply them to influencer accounts across platforms, and we add
dimensions that propaganda taxonomies do not provide, such as temporal framing and
account-level stability.

错误信息研究询问一项主张是否属实,以及虚假主张如何蔓延(Vosoughi等人,2018年). Clickbait 检测目标为扣号头条
(Pottast等人,2016年;Chen等人,2015年)。
精细的宣传检测标签技术,如装填语言和

标记区分不可靠与可靠的新闻(Rashkin等人,2017年). 我们借

账户水平稳定性。

blocks.en:
Computational studies of exaggeration model hyperbole as a lexical and semantic
phenomenon ( Troiano et al., 2018 ) and detect exaggerated causal claims in science
communication ( Wright and Augenstein, 2021 ) . Informal logic treats argumentative
hyperbole as a fallacy of proportion ( Kreider, 2022 ) . Our SI dimension adopts
this proportionality view and extends it to framing that inflates importance, urgency,
novelty, or emotional intensity.

a stand-alone classifier, we use it as a verifier gated by transparent rules, report how
often it overrides them, and validate its output against human annotators and a second
model.

Affordances are the action possibilities that a platform’s design, algorithms, and norms

Existing detectors are built for single platforms, single languages, or edited news, and
they treat the text attached to a post as one unit. It therefore remains unknown whether
disproportionate framing is primarily a property of topics, of platforms, or of the
audience layer that threaded platforms attach to creator posts. Answering this requires
an instrument that is applied identically across platforms and languages, that can be
run separately on creator and reply text, and whose labels are validated against human
judgment. This is the goal of our study.

blocks.en: 3.1. Dataset
blocks.zh: 3.1. 数据集

blocks.en:
We selected accounts purposively on six platforms that differ in format and interaction
design: RSS/newsletters (long-form, no replies), YouTube (title plus transcript excerpt),
Bluesky and X/Twitter (short-form, threaded), Reddit (community-moderated), and Weibo
(Chinese short-form). Accounts span ten content categories (AI/ML, finance, media,
politics, tech, science, health, culture, education, and startup) and a range of expected
distortion levels. For each account we collected its most recent 20–50 posts in July
2026: 20 per YouTube channel, up to 30 per RSS feed, and up to 50 elsewhere. RSS,
YouTube, and Bluesky were collected through public feeds and APIs. Reddit, X/Twitter, and
Weibo were collected through browser automation on publicly visible pages. For X/Twitter
we also stored the text of the top-5 replies to each post as ranked by the platform.

blocks.en: 3.2. Theoretical Framework and Indices
blocks.zh: 3.2. 理论框架和指数

blocks.en:
Following framing theory ( Entman, 1993 ) and the treatment of hyperbole as a
fallacy of proportion ( Kreider, 2022 ) , we define rhetorical distortion as framing whose salience, urgency, novelty, or emotional intensity exceeds what the
underlying information warrants. Our system does not verify the underlying evidence. It
detects linguistic markers that are characteristic of such framing, so all reported
rates are rates of distortion signals ; we return to this distinction in
§ 5 . We organize the markers using the Aristotelian appeals ( Aristotle, 1991 ) as operationalized for computational persuasion analysis ( Pauli et al., 2022 ) : • SI (logos) : language that inflates importance beyond
evidential support, which is salience manipulation in Entman’s sense ( Entman, 1993 ; Kreider, 2022 ) . Examples: “changes everything,” “once in a generation.” • AM (pathos) : fear appeals that target the reader’s own job,
money, skills, or future, based on the threat-severity and susceptibility
components of the Extended Parallel Process Model ( Witte, 1992 ; Witte and Allen, 2000 ) .
Examples: “you will be left behind,” “hope you’re prepared.” • NC (ethos) : claims of exclusivity, hidden knowledge, or
epistemic priority ( Flanagin and Metzger, 2017 ) , related to unwarranted appeals to
authority ( Da San Martino et al., 2019 ) . Examples: “nobody is talking about this.” • LL (pathos) : emotionally charged wording or typography whose
intensity exceeds the content ( Da San Martino et al., 2019 ; Weston, 2018 ) .
Examples: “catastrophic,” insults, ALL-CAPS shouting, “!!!”. • TD (logos) : explicit urgency labels such as “BREAKING” or
“just dropped,” operationalizing the timeliness dimension of information
quality ( Wang and Strong, 1996 ) .

blocks.en:
Four decisions make the dimensions operational and are shared by the rules, the LLM
prompts, and the annotation codebook. First, only the author’s own wording counts:
quoted speech, headlines of linked articles reported neutrally, and self-deprecating
jokes are not distortion. Second, a post may carry several dimensions, and each is
judged independently. Third, an intense adjective on its own (“insane,”
“staggering”) is LL, and it becomes SI only when the post also claims outsized
importance; factual superlatives stated with numbers (“largest IPO on record, valued at
$3.28T”) are neither. Fourth, AM requires that the reader be the target of the threat.
The author’s own fear, reports of disasters or market drops, and general political alarm
do not count, and TD requires an explicit urgency label rather than mere recency.

blocks.en: 3.3. Three-Tier Classification Pipeline
blocks.zh: 3.3. 三级管线

blocks.en:
The pipeline is designed around a division of labor (Figure 1 ). Lexical
rules are cheap, transparent, and identical across platforms, but they cannot judge
whether a matched phrase is used disproportionately. An LLM can make that judgment, but
applying it to every post would be costly and would make the labels depend entirely on an
opaque model. We therefore let the rules decide which posts are examined and let
the LLM decide what the labels are. The three tiers and the routing between them are
described below.

blocks.en: 3.4. Creator–Reply Decomposition
blocks.zh: 3.4. 创建者-还原分解

blocks.en:
The default X/Twitter unit merges a tweet with its top-5 replies, so its labels mix
creator and audience text. To separate the two, we run the full pipeline, with identical
rules, filters, paths, and prompts, a second time on each tweet alone and a third time on
its replies alone. Comparing the two on the same posts yields a paired creator–audience

blocks.en: 3.5. Validation

We validate the pipeline against two human annotators who labeled the five dimensions
independently, using the codebook of § 3.2 and blind to all system output.
The main sample contains 198 posts stratified by platform and by whether any pipeline
version flagged the post (33 per platform). Each stratum is weighted by its size in the
corpus divided by its size in the sample, so the metrics estimate corpus-level
performance. Following the codebook rule that only the author’s own wording counts, the
annotators labeled each X/Twitter item for its creator tweet and not for the attached
replies. We therefore score X/Twitter items against the pipeline’s tweet-only labels
(§ 3.4 ) and validate the reply layer with a second sample of 60
X/Twitter reply units (the top-5 replies of the 26 sampled tweets that had replies, plus
34 posts drawn at random from the analysis set), labeled by the same two annotators.
Agreement between the annotators is substantial: Cohen’s κ \kappa for any dimension is
0.76 in both samples; per dimension it is 0.69 (SI), 0.56 (AM), 0.78 (LL), and 1.00 for

The pipeline above is the result of a revision. A first audit, with an LLM annotator
(Anthropic’s Claude) blind to system output, exposed defects in an initial version of the
rule layer. An ALL-CAPS pattern compiled case-insensitively matched any word of four or
more letters and fired on 78% of posts. An “EVERYTHING” pattern matched any
“everything.” A two-weak-marker requirement kept single markers such as
“unprecedented” from ever reaching the LLM. Several generic Chinese markers
(“highest”/“largest”/“first”; Appendix B ) fired mostly on neutral news, and a filter match vetoed an entire
dimension. We fixed these defects, unified the rules across languages, and tightened the
LLM definitions. The human sample above was drawn after these changes and is disjoint
from the first audit. On its non-X/Twitter units, where both versions classify identical
text, human-judged any-dimension F1 rises from 0.24 for the initial pipeline to 0.52 for
the final one. The LLM annotator’s own labels agree with the humans only moderately
(any-dimension F1 0.60–0.61 on those units), so LLM-based audits are useful for finding
defects but overstate accuracy; we report human agreement throughout.

The remaining errors fall into a few recurring patterns. SI false positives are mostly
factual superlatives in news (records, “first” awards, “the largest model ever
released”) and Chinese markers such as “in history” and “historic” (Appendix B ) in
official reporting.
AM false negatives are personal-finance video titles that address the viewer’s money
without any listed marker (“Your money is about to be worth a lot less”), which never
pass the rule gate. These patterns suggest that SI and AM need content-level rather than
lexical cues, which we discuss in § 5 .

We present the results in the order of the research questions. We start with platform and

We close with an exploratory engagement analysis (§ 4.5 ) and an analysis

blocks.en: 4.3. Cross-Linguistic Transfer (RQ3)
blocks.zh: 4.3. 跨语言转移(RQ3)

blocks.en:
Weibo sits in the low tier (DI 0.97, indistinguishable from RSS and Reddit), with an
SI-led profile. Within matched categories, Weibo SI is lower than English for finance
(1.90% vs. 4.03%; 18 vs. 31 accounts, excluding crypto) but higher for AI/ML (7.20%
vs. 1.68%; 5 vs. 26 accounts). We do not interpret either comparison as a language
difference, for three reasons. First, Weibo posts are short (113 characters), and after
controlling for length Weibo’s odds of a flag exceed those of RSS (OR 2.34;
Table 7 ), reversing the raw ordering. Second, the error analysis found that
Chinese superlatives (“in history”, “historic”) are a frequent source of SI false positives
on factual news. Third, the Weibo sample is weighted toward official media and
institutional accounts. Cross-linguistic comparison therefore requires language-specific
calibration, which we leave to future work.

the RSS feeds of news organizations are section feeds (technology) rather than the

blocks.zh: 5.五. 讨论情况

blocks.en:
Here, we examine where rhetorical distortion is located across six platforms and two
languages. We find that platform is strongly associated with distortion level, that
platforms elevate different dimensions, and that on X/Twitter most of the measured
distortion comes from the reply layer rather than from creators. We discuss what these
findings imply for how distortion arises, for the measurement pipeline, and for
platforms.

The answer to RQ1 is that platform is strongly associated with distortion level and
category only weakly, with category differences confined largely to X/Twitter. The
decomposition (RQ4) refines the affordance account. On a threaded platform, most of the
measured distortion comes from the reply layer that the platform ranks and attaches to a
creator’s post; X/Twitter creators themselves write at the level of YouTube and Bluesky.
Among creator-authored text, YouTube stands out, and its high SI is consistent with a
format that rewards framing a video as significant. Platform-level comparisons that merge
creator and audience text can therefore overstate creator distortion on threaded
platforms, and we recommend reporting the two layers separately.

blocks.en:
Three mechanisms could produce the creator–reply gap, and our data cannot yet separate
them. First, ranking: the replies we observe are the five the platform chose to show, and
ranking that favors engagement would surface the most emotional ones ( Brady et al., 2017 ) . Second, audience composition: replies to political and media
accounts draw partisan audiences, and out-group animosity is itself engaging ( Rathje et al., 2021 ) ; the largest gaps in our data are indeed in politics (2.5 vs. 12.5) and media (2.0 vs. 8.5). Third, norms: comment sections have long shown high
incivility independently of ranking ( Coe et al., 2014 ) . The length-controlled
comparison adds a fourth, mechanical contribution: much of the reply-layer gap comes from
the aggregation of several replies, although individual replies still carry more loaded
language than the tweets they answer. Distinguishing these mechanisms would require
replies in chronological as well as ranked order, which is a direct extension of our
collection.

The stage decomposition (§ 4.6 ) suggests a practical division of labor. For
dimensions with clear lexical markers (TD, LL), the rules supply candidates and the LLM
acts as a precision filter, discarding about 40% of them; against human labels this
combination is precise (TD 0.77, LL 0.71) though conservative for LL. For dimensions
defined by communicative intent rather than wording (AM and, to a lesser extent, SI), the
rules rarely fire, and most labels are the LLM’s own inferences on posts it saw for
another reason. The human annotators rarely shared these inferences for AM. A system
aimed at AM therefore needs either intent-level training data or a dedicated LLM pass
with its own validation, rather than piggybacking on an LL gate.

blocks.en:
For information literacy, the results suggest that platform-specific reading strategies
(for example, discounting reply-thread framing) may transfer better than topic-specific
skepticism. For platform governance, the reply layer is where emotionally loaded framing
concentrates around otherwise neutral news posts, which makes reply ranking a natural
point of intervention. For measurement, our experience suggests five practices for
similar systems. (1) Classify creator and audience text separately on threaded
platforms; merging them changed X/Twitter’s apparent creator distortion by a factor of
3.6. Report reply-layer and per-reply measures separately, since aggregation alone more
than doubles the reply-layer rate. (2) Report dimensions individually, because the
composite hides which strategy dominates and because reliability differs sharply by
dimension. (3) Control for text length when comparing platforms, since length alone
roughly doubles the odds of a flag per unit of log length. (4) Audit the rule layer, not
only the LLM: in our case the largest errors were silent defects in the gate, invisible
from the final labels alone. (5) Validate against humans rather than another LLM, since
LLM-based audits overstated accuracy in our case.

blocks.en:
Our results point to several directions for future research. Measurement validity. The system detects linguistic markers of disproportionate
framing. It does not verify that framing exceeds the evidence, and a genuinely breaking
story legitimately uses “breaking.” Human agreement is good for TD, moderate for SI and
LL, and poor for NC and AM, so NC and AM rates are exploratory; 89% of final AM labels
are LLM additions that no rule proposed (§ 4.6 ). The validation samples are
small (198 posts and 60 reply units, two annotators), and with 33 posts per platform they
are too small to estimate platform-level human prevalence precisely; they suggest that
pipeline recall is lower on YouTube titles than on other text. Recall gate. No post is labeled without a rule hit, so recall is bounded by the
rule lists; this matters most for Chinese. Reply layer. Only X/Twitter replies were collected, so we cannot say whether
Reddit, Bluesky, or YouTube comments show the same pattern. The top-5 replies are ranked
by the platform. The length-controlled comparison (Table 11 ) shows that
most of the reply-layer gap reflects aggregation; the per-reply excess (1.5 × \times ) is
smaller and rests mainly on LL. Sampling. Accounts were chosen purposively, with 20–50 recent posts each, which
limits population-level inference; all findings are associational. YouTube’s 20-post
windows make CS less informative there (mean 0.50). Model dependence. Labels depend on proprietary models whose behavior may change
across versions. The ordering and the reply gap replicate with GPT-4o, but platform-level
DI is 10–42% lower under GPT-4o, so levels should not be compared across models.
Future work will improve AM and NC detection, collect comment layers on other platforms,
and extend Chinese marker coverage with language-specific calibration.

blocks.en: 6. Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6个 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced a five-dimension, literature-grounded framework for rhetorical distortion
and a three-tier pipeline in which transparent rules select candidates and an LLM assigns
labels, and we measured distortion on 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on six platforms in
two languages. Platform is far more strongly associated with distortion level than topic.
X/Twitter scores highest, but classifying tweets and replies separately shows that the
reply layer under a post carries 3.5 × \times the distortion of the tweet it answers
(1.5 × \times at equal length, mostly loaded language), while creator tweets resemble
YouTube and Bluesky. Human annotators and a second classifier (GPT-4o) confirm the reply
gap. Measuring creator and audience text separately is therefore essential for
understanding where disproportionate framing lives on threaded platforms.
